doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Touring Europe with Hampton, Frankie Dunlop and 'When You're Smiling'
summary: He read Hampton's book well but played high notes, learned bebop drumming from Frankie Dunlop, and Hampton had him play 'When You're Smiling' in Armstrong's style.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: There’s a lot of music in college that you won’t play anywhere else, because the music just takes so long to prepare. In other words, not to get on another tangent, it’s about time when you get in a professional arena, if you go to the Chicago Symphony, well let me give a better example. When you go play a show somewhere, they’re going to try and make the music not so difficult because they might have an hour, two hours at the most, to rehearse it. They can’t give you a bunch of incredibly hard stuff, they’re going to give you something that is pretty readable. So I’d been playing this music that was impossible, all these time changes and really counting and doing all this stuff, and also very jazz but stiff. But my reading was — because at Eastman you read every day and it’s tough stuff too. So I go to this thing and I’m reading my ass off because I’m used to reading this hard stuff. And the only thing I’m lacking is a good feel, I’m playing a little stiff, but the guys are looking at me like, “Wow, this cat really reads well.” It comes time for my first solo, I said I’ve got to get this gig, and this man wants to hear some high notes, so I’m like blaaahh — and the cats are looking at me like what’s this cat playing all these high notes, that’s not too tasty. But I’m trying to get the gig. So he liked it and so then I left school even before I took my finals, and I told my parents I said oh I can make them up and I’ll take them later, and I never did. But I got to go on a six week tour of Europe with Lionel Hampton’s band, a guy named Frankie Dunlop was the drummer, formerly with Thelonious Monk, an incredible drummer. It was the first time I realized that a drum could be a melodic instrument. He’d play solos every night and I’d end up singing them when I got off stage. He’d play like [scats] It’s like stuff like that. He was playing bebop on the drums. And I’d never heard — you know whenever I knew drummers solo, other than when I listened to like Max Roach with Clifford, it was like yeah I can sing that. But to be on stage with a guy that was playing bebop on the drums, it was like he would play songs [scats]. You know that song “Red Cross?” [scats] He’d be playing that, and he’d play bebop on the drums. And I was like wow! Because before when I’d hear kids play drum solos or in school and stuff it was like somebody was throwing some pots and pans down the stairs you know. And here was like this guy was playing music on the drums. So between him and hearing Lionel Hampton play every night which was incredible, and

watching how he integrated entertainment into the whole thing was interesting. And then Lionel was the first guy, we’re running a little short here, but Lionel was the first guy that he heard me playing and he said, “Yeah sometimes you sound like Louis Armstrong.” And I had had a little, I always loved Louis, but he wasn’t like my main thing, my man was Kenny Dorham and Lee Morgan. But I always loved Louis Armstrong. He said, “You know I recorded with Louis Armstrong.” I said, “Of course, I know.” He said, “Let’s play, you and me, ‘When You’re Smiling.’” Because when Louis would play that it would seem like when he got to that last note it was the highest note in the world. So he says, “When you play it I want you to do that.” So I started playing “When You’re Smiling” with Lionel, we would just do it once a night. And his whole thing is, “I’m gonna’ make you a star.” He used to tell everybody that. Make you a star. Or he would say, “Stick with me, Gates, I’m gonna make some money, you dig?” So he would really say that I swear. So we started playing “When You’re Smiling” and it started me listening to Louis again. I always had heard stuff — and really going back and focusing on him. Plus that feeling of Louis was in Lionel’s playing, that happiness, that was in Lionel’s playing too. So that’s when I started getting a little bit into enjoying the music of Louis a little bit more.
I had heard it in your playing last night every once in a while.
